subject: Science
chapter: Chapter 10: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
central_question: How does the human eye form clear images, how are common vision defects corrected, and how do refraction, dispersion, atmospheric refraction and scattering produce familiar optical phenomena?
in_scope_units: The human eye: cornea, iris, pupil, crystalline lens, retina, optic nerve and image formation.
Power of accommodation, near point, far point and cataract.
Defects of vision and their correction: myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia.
Refraction of light through a triangular glass prism and angle of deviation.
Dispersion of white light, spectrum, VIBGYOR, recombination and rainbow formation.
Atmospheric refraction: wavering through hot air, twinkling of stars, non-twinkling of planets, advanced sunrise and delayed sunset.
Scattering of light, Tyndall effect, blue colour of the sky and use of red danger signals.
banned_topics: Detailed mirror formula and image formation by spherical mirrors, which belong to the previous light chapter.
Detailed lens formula derivations and ray-diagram cases for lenses beyond what is needed for vision correction.
Wave optics topics such as interference, diffraction and polarisation.
Detailed anatomy or diseases of the eye not discussed in this chapter.

known_pitfalls.claim: The eye lens performs most of the refraction of incoming light.
known_pitfalls.correction: Most refraction occurs at the outer surface of the cornea; the crystalline lens mainly provides fine adjustment of focal length for focusing on the retina.

known_pitfalls.claim: Myopia is corrected by a convex lens because the image forms in front of the retina.
known_pitfalls.correction: Myopia is corrected by a concave lens, which diverges incoming rays so that the eye focuses the image on the retina.

known_pitfalls.claim: Hypermetropia and presbyopia are the same defect.
known_pitfalls.correction: Hypermetropia is a refractive defect caused by an eye lens with too long a focal length or a short eyeball; presbyopia is an age-related loss of accommodation due to weakening ciliary muscles and reduced lens flexibility.

known_pitfalls.claim: Stars twinkle because they produce changing amounts of light.
known_pitfalls.correction: Stars twinkle because atmospheric refraction through continually changing layers of air changes their apparent position and the amount of starlight entering the eye.

known_pitfalls.claim: The sky is blue because the atmosphere contains blue-coloured particles.
known_pitfalls.correction: Fine particles and air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths, especially blue light, more strongly than longer red wavelengths.
